lines.text: This flat Starlink dish is talking to a satellite racing across the sky, and it never turns to follow it.
That satellite flies about 480 km above you, and in a few minutes it slips below the horizon. So how does a dish that never moves keep up?
So here's the trip every video you watch on it makes: up from the dish, to the satellite, down to a ground station, and into the internet.
On the way we'll open the dish, watch it bend a beam with no moving parts, and see why it takes so many satellites.
For decades, satellite internet and TV worked another way. Look at the dishes on this street.
Every one of them points at the same spot in the sky: one satellite, 35,786 km above the equator.
Why that height? Up there, one trip around the Earth takes as long as the Earth takes to turn once.
That's why every TV dish on a street faces the same way: they're all staring at one fixed point in the sky.
So the satellite seems to hang still, and the dish can be bolted in place, aimed once, and left alone.
That's fine for TV. But what happens when you're on a video call?
So what's wrong with that? Distance. Your click has to climb all the way up to that satellite, and all the way back down.
Radio moves at the speed of light, but that's still a long trip, and a web page needs many of them, one after another.
You feel it. On a video call, people talk over each other, because every word arrives a beat late.
So what if the satellite flew lower? Bring it down, to about 480 km.
That's only 1.3% of the old height. The trip up and back shrinks to the same small share.
Light covers that short hop so fast that the distance stops being the slow part of the trip.
So the delay drops from something you notice to something you don't.
But low comes with a catch. A satellite this low can't hang still.
Why not? Down here it has to race around the planet to stay up, so it crosses your sky in minutes.
To follow it, an old dish would have to swing across the whole sky, again and again, all day.
Starlink's flat dish doesn't move at all. So what is inside it?
Here it is on a workbench. On the outside, it's just a flat white panel on a stand, with one cable.
Lift the white cover, and there's no curved mirror inside, like a TV dish has.
The cover is plastic for a reason: radio passes straight through it, while rain and snow stay out.
So what is there instead? A board, covered in a grid of many tiny antennas, each one a small flat metal patch.
Each patch can send and hear radio on its own, but one by itself is too small to aim at anything.
So who tells each one when to fire? The chips underneath. They control every antenna's timing, down to a tiny fraction of a second.
The dish's one cable runs down to the router inside. The router plugs into the wall for its power.
From there, the router turns it into wifi, for your laptop and the phone in your hand.
One patch can't aim. Many working together can. Here's how.
Here's the trick, drawn wave by wave. Line up a row of the antennas.
When they all send at the same instant, their ripples add up into one strong wave, heading straight up.
Now make each antenna fire a little later than the one beside it.
Think of a row of people clapping. Clap together and the sound goes straight ahead. Clap one after another, and it heads off at an angle.
So what happens to the wave? The ripples still add up, but now the wave front tilts, and the beam leans over toward the late side.
Change the delays, and the beam swings across the sky. Nothing turns. Nothing moves. It's aiming by timing.
Engineers call this a phased array. The dish does it with its whole grid at once, in every direction.
And because it's only timing, it can change its aim far faster than any motor could swing a dish.
So far: the satellites fly low to keep the trip short, and the dish follows them by timing, not turning.
But there's a problem no timing can fix. In a few minutes, your satellite drops below the horizon.
So the dish hands off. Before the first satellite sets, the next one is already rising.
The chips change the timing, and in a blink the beam jumps from the old satellite to the new one.
Does your video stop? No. Most of the time, the handoff happens too fast to notice.
And it happens again and again, all day and all night, for every dish under the sky.
And here's the surprise. The satellite is doing the same trick. Each one carries 5 phased arrays of its own.
Its beams sweep the ground below, each one serving the dishes in a patch of land at a time.
Then it passes your signal down to a ground station, which is wired into the internet.
But one satellite only ever covers a small patch of the planet. So how do you get a signal everywhere?
Starlink's first 60 working satellites went up together, on one rocket, in 2019.
They spread out into a long line, like beads on a string, then climbed up to their places.
Did one launch do it? No. Since then, launch after launch has filled the low sky with a moving web of them.
Each group flies its own tilted path, so between them, the rings of satellites wrap the whole planet.
That's why the sky above your house is never empty: one is always rising as another one sets.
So follow your video one last time. You press play, and the laptop asks for it over wifi.
The router sends it up the cable, and the dish works out where your satellite is right now.
Its tiny antennas fire a fraction apart, and the beam leans up to a satellite 480 km overhead.
The satellite catches it on one of its arrays, and points another beam down to the ground.
Into the internet through the ground station, and your video rides the same path back to you.
All in a blink. From a flat dish that never moves, aimed at satellites that never stop.
Which machine should we take apart next? Tell us. Until then, look up: one is crossing your sky right now.

craft_problems: note: four shots in a row open wide (from 'hook2'): vary the shot size
note: 30 s without a close or extreme shot (at most 15 s): emotion lives in close-ups
note: only 1 kinds of scene (directed); a long video mixes 5+ (build, framework, type, journey, stats, case, custom...) so it never settles into one look
note: directed is 60 of 60 composed beats (at most 40%): vary how each idea is shown
note: directed 4 times in a row: change the device
